chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.citation: Meng, J et al. (2022). Determining Factors for Nitrite Accumulation in an Acidic Nitrifying System: Influent Ammonium Concentration, Operational pH, and Ammonia-Oxidizing Community. nan.
chunks.text: Nitrification is an essential process for nitrogen removal from wastewater, comprising two steps, i.e., the oxidation of ammonium (NH 4 + ) to nitrite (NO 2 − ), and then to nitrate (NO 3 − ). In a wastewater treatment system, nitrification usually occurs at a neutral pH (∼7) with NO 3 − as the final product when the oxygen supply is unlimited. Nitrification at an acidic pH was recently suggested as a novel process for wastewater treatment. At a slightly acidic pH range (4.5−5.5), it was found that the end product of nitrification tends to be NO 2 − instead of NO 3 − , even with high dissolved oxygen (DO > 4 mg O 2 / L). 1,2 However, acidic nitrification without considerable NO 2 − accumulation has also been widely reported in literature. 3−5 Tarre et al. 4 observed NO 3 − accumulation in suspended-and attached-biomass reactors at pH of ∼4, in which nitriteoxidizing bacteria (NOB) Nitrobacter existed in large aggregates.

chunks.citation: Ma, Y et al. (2009). Achieving nitrogen removal via nitrite in a pilot-scale continuous pre-denitrification plant. nan.
chunks.text:
The traditional biological nitrogen removal processes utilized in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) involve the oxidation of ammonium (NH 4 þ ) to nitrate (NO 3 À ) (nitrification) followed by nitrate reduction with an organic carbon source to nitrogen gas (N 2 ) (denitrification). Both nitrification and denitrification possess nitrite (NO 2 À ) as an intermediate. Hence, if

nitrification is stopped at nitrite, denitritation from nitrite to nitrogen gas can be achieved (Verstraete et al., 1977) . Nitrogen removal via nitrite yields 25% reduction in oxygen demand for nitrification and 40% reduction in chemical oxygen demand (COD) requirement for denitrification (Pollice et al., 2002; Turk and Mavinic, 1987) . The reduction in COD requirement would be particularly advantageous for WWTPs treating wastewater with a low COD to nitrogen ratio.

chunks.text: In order to recover the lipid-rich biomass from the treated wastewaters and to further reduce the level of COD in the respective wastewaters, microfiltration using a low-cost ceramic membrane (pore size: 1.01 μm and porosity: 44%) was carried out. Fig. 6 presents the membrane flux and COD removal (%) from the different wastewaters at various operating pressures in the range of 34-172 kPa. With an increase in the operating pressure, the flux of the microfiltration system increased due to a high driving force acting on the membrane surface. The membrane flux was lower for DWW and PPWW as compared with that for the BGWW due to membrane fouling. In general, the membrane fouling is attributed to concentration polarization on the membrane surface and blocking of pores in the porous ceramic structure. In case of DWW and PPWW, fouling of the membrane was observed due to the adsorption of organic solutes/lignin and membrane surface polarization that creates further resistance to the transport of liquid through the membrane [1] . On the other hand, the less viscous BGWW possesses persistent organics [22] , and hence do not affect the membrane flux largely.

chunks.text: Water is one of the most important resources for human survival. The water demand has pronounced over the past decades due to population growth, industry development, and agricultural expansion. Although groundwater, surface water, and rainwater are conventional freshwater resources, nowadays, unconventional water resources such as wastewater are recognized as valuable resources for freshwater supply. In this regard, wastewater treatment and reuse have become viable selections for providing additional water supplies (Kim and Jang, 2006) . Membrane bioreactor (MBR) systems are one of the most promising wastewater treatment technologies growing increasingly all over the world, especially in developing countries (Wu et al., 2008) . Membrane bioreactors combine conventional activated sludge (CAS) and membrane separation technologies to produce high-quality water (Zhang et al., 2021) . MBR technology reduces plant footprint by eliminating clarifiers and conventional filters, which makes them more efficient in comparison with conventional wastewater treatment processes (Judd, 2010; Deng et al., 2015) .

Wastewater samples were then exposed to UV fluences between 10 and 60 mJ/cm 2 . Following treatment, samples were enumerated for E. coli and total coliforms. Pre-and post-UV exposure samples collected at the wastewater treatment facility were also enumerated as controls. All samples were collected as singlets per event and processed under subdued red light to reduce the effects of photo-reactivation.

chunks.text: The sewer-mining unit consists of two sub-units; the Membrane bioreactor (MBR) and the Reverse Osmosis (RO) unit. Both have been constructed as individual packaged modules that are joined together in one compact system offering ease of transportation. The capacity of the unit is 10 m 3 /d. In the MBR, a circulation stream of sludge keeps in balance the biological solids around the membranes. This recirculation stream is rich in dissolved oxygen (2.5e5.0 mgO 2 /L) and provides to the nitrification zone supplemental oxygen for the biological processes. This stream also prevents the sludge de-watering in the filtration tank and additionally reduces the fouling of the membranes by reducing the TSS load at the membrane. The circulation rate regulates the biomass concentration, which should not exceed a maximum threshold. MBR operation requires that this stream is 4 times the net permeate flow. The latter suggests an overall sludge circulation flow of 40 m 3 /d during the peak flow. For the maintenance of the membrane, the standard suction required for sludge filtration is periodically interrupted for a backflush and/or a relaxation cycle ("Cleaning in place").

chunks.text: The nitritation is a common attempt for generating NO 2 − -N for anammox bacteria. This process consists of two pivots: enrichment of AOB and suppression of nitrite oxidizing bacteria (NOB) by making selective pressure on the two groups of bacteria (Fig. 1 ). The primary strategies for controlling nitritation include low dissolved oxygen (DO) (Laureni et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2013) , high temperature, short sludge retention time (SRT) (Kouba et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2013; Pollice et al., 2002) , real-time aeration control (Gu et al., 2012; Peng et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2007) , as well as the free ammonia (FA) and free nitrous acid (FNA) based sludge treatment (Wang et al., 2016) . However, there are still major issues in the practical application for both of the high-strength wastewater and mainstream treatment.

chunks.text: Nitrogen removal in conventional wastewater treatment is primarily accomplished through nitrification/denitrification (N/DN) (Arumugham et al., 2024) . However, this process requires aeration and carbon sources, and produces CO 2 and N 2 O (Cao and Fan, 2023) . Wastewater treatment facilities produce 1-2 % of society's total carbon dioxide emissions (Zhang et al., 2024b) , and 3 % of global N 2 O (Ramírez-Melgarejo et al., 2020) . In contrast, anammox utilizes nitrite as an electron acceptor to directly convert NH 4 + to N 2 , reducing N 2 O emissions, reducing oxygen consumption by 62.5 %, eliminating the need for carbon inputs, and reducing sludge production by 90 % (Huang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2019a) .

chunks.text: A pilot scale ceramic cross flow microfiltration (MF) system (Fig. 1 ) was used for pig manure filtration. The MF system primarily consisted of controlling valves, pumps, membrane modules, manometer, flowmeters, thermometer, temperature controller and a programmable logical controller (PLC) system. An external tank of 100 L volume was used as feed tank for the experiment. A ceramic MF membrane (Al 2 O 3 , inopore GmbH, Germany) module of 0.2 µm pore size and 1 m Length was used for the filtration. The effective membrane area was 0.158 m 2 .

chunks.citation: Wei, CH et al. (2014). Sustainable organic loading rate and energy recovery potential of mesophilic anaerobic membrane bioreactor for municipal wastewater treatment. BIORESOURCE TECHNOL.
chunks.text: An anaerobic membrane bioreactor (AnMBR) -a hybrid of anaerobic digestion and membrane separation -may overcome the drawbacks of the conventional anaerobic activated sludge process through the excellent sludge-water separation by a microfiltration (MF) or ultrafiltration (UF) membrane. The coupling of a membrane results in high biomass (and thus high OLR and organics removal), and produces a good quality effluent that has significantly lower amount of particles and pathogens (Liao et al., 2006) . Several recent reviews on published AnMBR studies over the past two decades show that AnMBR can achieve high COD removal (more than 85%, up to 99%) with low permeate COD (less than 100 mg/L, down to below 10 mg/L) under a range of hydraulic retention time (HRT) of 3-120 h, sludge retention time (SRT) of 15 d to infinity, volumetric OLR of 0.2-5 gCOD/L/d and operating temperature of 10-37 °C for real and/or synthetic municipal wastewater treatment (Lin et al., 2013; Ozgun et al., 2013; Skouteris et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2012; Stuckey, 2012) .
